 A federal judge and a top Justice Department official butted heads over the political appointee’s involvement in litigation over a Washington community golf course, with the judge asking other government attorneys to raise their hands if they would sign a recent filing.
 The testy exchange between Judge Ana Reyes of the US District Court for the District of Columbia and Associate Attorney General Stanley Woodward played out during a Monday hearing in a legal challenge to President Donald Trump’s proposed changes to the East Potomac Park golf course. 
 The case is one of several efforts by Trump to reshape Washington’s historic landmarks in his own image, including by attempting to rename the Kennedy Center for himself and building a massive new White House ballroom using private donations. Hours before the hearing, Trump wrote in a social media post that Reyes is a “crazed lunatic” and that work on the golf course would start “immediately.” 
 Reyes, a Joe Biden appointee, initially ordered the federal government to resubmit a recent court filing signed only by Woodward, a political appointee, with the signatures of any attorneys who have appeared in the case who are willing to sign on. She then turned to the counsel’s table in the courtroom and suggested any attorneys willing to join Woodward on the brief raise their hands.
 Woodward told Reyes this wasn’t an “appropriate ask” and instructed the government lawyers not to answer. 
 “I’m giving them a direct order,” Reyes replied. After Woodward said the request put the lawyers in an “untenable” position, Reyes ordered the government to submit a brief on this issue. 
 Read more: Trump DOJ Relies on Politically Appointed Lawyers in Major Cases 
 The dispute stems from a legal challenge, filed in February by a historic preservation organization and two Washington area residents, to potential changes to the golf course, a public park established in 1897. The lawsuit argues the administration is bypassing environmental and preservation requirements. 
 The administration has plowed forward with potential changes to the golf course. Trump, in a social media post earlier Sunday, announced plans to create a “World Class Championship Golf Course” in East Potomac Park, with work expected to begin Nov. 15. The golf course, he wrote, is “completely overgrown, dysfunctional, and unsafe.”
 Gregory Wischer, deputy chief of staff for the Interior Department, testified during the Monday hearing that recent actions to cut down trees in the public park are part of “cleaning up the course” under a 2019 landscaping plan. Other officials are expected to testify later Monday.
 Reyes also questioned Justice Department lawyer Robert Stander about whether it was a “coincidence” that the government decided to act on the seven-year-old landscaping plan after Trump requested changes to the golf course. Stander said he didn’t know the answer to that and that he has “no reason to believe” the government’s past representations in court weren’t accurate.
 The case is the latest flashpoint as tensions escalate between the Trump administration and the federal judiciary. The night before, Reyes rejected Woodward’s request to recuse from the golf course case.
 Woodward had accused the judge of demonstrating bias toward the government during a recent court hearing. He argued late Friday that Reyes showed “deep-seated and unequivocal antipathy” toward the Trump administration during the hearing, in which Reyes chastised a DOJ attorney for the government’s conduct in the case.
 Reyes rebutted the Justice Department’s allegations claim-by-claim, citing portions of transcripts from prior court hearings in which the judge praised the government lawyers and refrained from ruling against the administration at earlier stages.
 “It is easy to weaponize selective quotations to bring a baseless recusal motion,” Reyes wrote in a 13-page opinion late Sunday. “But it is much harder to meet the demanding legal standard against a full record.” 
 The recusal request came after Reyes tore into a government lawyer during a heated Oct. 12 hearing for failing to notify her sufficiently in advance before cutting down hundreds of trees from the park over a holiday weekend.
 Reyes told DOJ lawyer Marissa Piropato at the remote hearing, convened on a federal holiday, she was “furious” the government had moved forward with tree removal despite her repeated requests for sufficient notice before major changes to the park. 
 The judge also said the government’s failure to alert the court sooner has cost it “all of its credibility” in this case.
 Woodward, told the court in a separate filing Sunday, with only his name on it, that plans for the golf course are not final, despite Trump’s announcement, and thus can’t be challenged in court under administrative law.
 The case is DC Preservation League v. Department of the Interior, D.D.C., No. 1:26-cv-00477, 10/18/26.
 ( Updates throughout with information from Monday hearing. )
